seoTitle: Trump tariff Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Trump tariff: work out product's potential price with reciprocal tariffs from the percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer and the current…
summary: Supply the percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer and the current price and the Trump tariff calculator solves for product's potential price with reciprocal tariffs. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Trump tariff calculator work?
sections.html:
The Trump tariff calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports product's potential price with reciprocal tariffs in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the product categories, the other product categories and the first, choose a product); then you type in the percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer, the current price (2), the potential price with reciprocal tariffs and the potential price with reciprocal tariffs (2).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Trump tariff calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Product's potential price with reciprocal tariffs=((who pays cbox < 1) ? ( product's current price × (base tariff rate × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + additional Trump tariff × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + 1) ÷ (base tariff rate × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + 1) ) : ( product's current price × (base tariff rate × (1) + additional Trump tariff × (1) + 1) ÷ (base tariff rate × (1) + 1) ))
Car's potential price with reciprocal tariffs=((who pays cbox < 1) ? ( car's current price × (car base tariff rate × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + additional Trump tariff × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + 1) ÷ (car base tariff rate × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + 1) ) : ( car's current price × (car base tariff rate × (1) + additional Trump tariff × (1) + 1) ÷ (car base tariff rate × (1) + 1) ))
Additional Trump tariff=((who pays cbox < 1) ? ( (potential price with reciprocal tariffs × pop base tariff rate × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + potential price with reciprocal tariffs − current price × pop base tariff rate × percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer − current price) ÷ (current price × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer)) ) : ( (potential price with reciprocal tariffs × pop base tariff rate × (1) + potential price with reciprocal tariffs − current price × pop base tariff rate × percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer − current price) ÷ (current price × (1)) ))
Additional Trump tariff=((who pays cbox < 1) ? ( (potential price with reciprocal tariffs − current price + pop base tariff rate × (potential price with reciprocal tariffs − current price) × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer)) ÷ (current price × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer)) ) : ( (potential price with reciprocal tariffs − current price + pop base tariff rate × (potential price with reciprocal tariffs − current price) × (1)) ÷ (current price × (1)) ))
Clothing's current price=((who pays cbox < 1) ? ( clothing's potential price with reciprocal tariffs × (clothes base tariff rate × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + 1) ÷ (clothes base tariff rate × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + additional Trump tariff × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + 1) ) : ( clothing's potential price with reciprocal tariffs × (clothes base tariff rate × (1) + 1) ÷ (clothes base tariff rate × (1) + additional Trump tariff × (1) + 1) ))
Electrical item's potential price with reciprocal tariffs=((who pays cbox < 1) ? ( electrical item's current price × (electronics base tariff rate × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + electronics tariff rate × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + 1) ÷ (electronics base tariff rate × (percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer) + 1) ) : ( electrical item's current price × (electronics base tariff rate × (1) + electronics tariff rate × (1) + 1) ÷ (electronics base tariff rate × (1) + 1) ))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Trump tariff calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer and the current price — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Trump tariff calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns product's potential price with reciprocal tariffs, derived from the percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer and the current price. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Trump tariff calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the percentage of tariffs passed on to you, the consumer and the current price, which is 16 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter additional Trump tariff in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Additional Trump tariff opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (7 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Additional Trump tariff = 0 %. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Trump tariff calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
